claims.claim: Frost heave is driven chiefly by liquid-water migration toward a freezing zone and the formation and thickening of segregated ice lenses, not merely by pore water freezing in place.
Frozen soil can contain both frozen and unfrozen water, with the proportions depending on temperature depression, soil specific surface area, and salt content.
Unfrozen liquid water can migrate vertically during freezing and feed the growth of horizontal layers of solid ice called ice lenses.
Ice lenses can separate soil above from soil below and produce large vertical ground displacements called frost heave.
Three conditions govern damaging frost action: freezing conditions, an available water supply, and frost-susceptible soil; not every wet or frozen soil heaves equally.
Soil type and mineralogy, groundwater and flow properties, moisture content, temperature, salinity, and material properties influence freezing behavior and frost-heave severity.
Fine-grained frost-susceptible soils can support more damaging frost action than many coarser soils, but susceptibility depends on the complete soil-water-freezing system rather than texture alone.
Frost heave can lift and damage pavement, producing roughness, displacement, and cracking above the growing ice-lens zone.
Freeze-thaw state in pavement layers can be investigated using subsurface temperature, moisture measurements such as time-domain reflectometry, and coupled heat-moisture models.
During thaw, ice lenses melt and previously heaved ground may lose support or settle unevenly; the exact outcome varies with soil, drainage, loading, and freeze-thaw history.

claims.claim: Pseudacteon tricuspis is a real phorid fly species whose larvae are solitary parasitoids of imported fire-ant workers, including the red imported fire ant Solenopsis invicta.
The adult female is a small hump-backed fly with reduced wing venation and a specialized external ovipositor.
A female can hover several millimeters above a fire-ant worker and make a rapid aerial strike that inserts an egg into the worker's thorax.
After hatching, the first instar develops in the thorax; a later instar migrates into the ant's head.
The third instar consumes tissue in the head capsule before pupariation, killing the worker.
Near pupariation, the late larva appears to release a substance, likely an enzyme, that degrades membranes holding the ant exoskeleton together and allows the head to detach.

The larva uses the detached ant head capsule as a protective chamber for pupariation; its hardened anterior plate occupies the oral opening and paired respiratory structures can extend from the puparium.
The adult fly eventually emerges through the detached ant head capsule.
Pseudacteon flies are much smaller than their fire-ant hosts, so the infographic should show the fly hovering close to the ant rather than at monster scale.
The presence of attacking Pseudacteon flies can interrupt imported fire-ant foraging by triggering defensive or evasive behavior, but this does not imply universal or complete colony control.
Pseudacteon tricuspis is native to South America and was introduced in the United States as a biological-control agent against imported fire ants.

sources.title: Fluorescent proteins in dominant mesophotic reef-building corals
The role of host pigments in coral photobiology

claims.claim: Many coral host pigments are green-fluorescent-protein-like pigments, and fluorescent forms span cyan, green, and red emission colors.
A fluorescent protein absorbs higher-energy light and emits lower-energy light at a longer wavelength.
Non-fluorescent chromoproteins can absorb visible light strongly while producing little or no fluorescence, and commonly contribute purple-blue coloration.
The pigment types and their expression can differ among coral species and among individuals of the same species.

Coral host pigments can alter the local light field inside coral tissue; proposed photobiological effects include photoprotection or light enhancement depending on species and environment, but their precise biological roles are not fully resolved.

In four Hawaiian mesophotic Leptoseris species studied at 65-125 m, cyan and green fluorescence was localized mainly in the coenosarc and/or oral disc, and fluorescent and non-fluorescent colonies co-occurred across the investigated depths.
In that Leptoseris study, cyan fluorescent protein was more common at shallower sampled depths, green fluorescent protein at deeper sampled depths, and both occurred at intermediate sampled depths.

The Leptoseris study found similar symbiont genotypes, abundance, pigments, photosynthetic efficiency, photosynthetic rates, and chlorophyll excitation spectra in fluorescent and non-fluorescent corals, so those fluorescent proteins were unlikely to significantly enhance symbiont photosynthesis in the studied corals.

Coral tissue can contain intracellular dinoflagellate photosymbionts in the endodermis, while host fluorescent pigments occupy species-dependent tissue locations and modify the light microenvironment around them.

claims.claim: Colobopsis explodens is a real ant species in the Southeast Asian Colobopsis cylindrica species group and was described from material associated with Borneo, Thailand, and Malaysia.
Field observations of Colobopsis explodens were made in lowland dipterocarp rainforest in Brunei, where colonies occupied trees and wooden nest cavities.
Minor workers are reddish-brown, measure about 4-7 mm, and carry enlarged mandibular-gland reservoirs extending through much of the body.
During close territorial conflict, a minor worker can rupture the integument of its gaster, an irreversible self-sacrificial behavior called autothysis.
Autothysis releases bright yellow, sticky mandibular-gland reservoir contents onto an arthropod opponent, helping restrain, repel, or kill the opponent.
The defensive sequence is a close-contact mechanism, not a fireball or pressure explosion: the gaster ruptures and transfers adhesive secretion to the opponent.
Major workers have enlarged plug-shaped heads and can block entrances to wooden nests, a defensive behavior known as phragmosis.
Chemical analyses found a complex mixture of volatile compounds in the minor workers' mandibular-gland reservoir contents, including alkanes, carboxylic acids, and phenolic compounds.

Researchers proposed that likely irritant and antibiotic phenolic constituents may contribute to defense against arthropod opponents or microbes, but the functions of many individual compounds remain unresolved.
The self-sacrificial rupture behavior belongs to minor workers and should not be implied to occur in every caste or every encounter.
